paper_title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Hidden states in decoder-only LLMs capture the progressive transformation of token representations through depth. While prior studies analyze individual layers through rank, sparsity, and entropy, modern inference pipelines increasingly use multiple target-model hidden states jointly. In speculative decoding methods such as EAGLE3, selected target-model layers are fused and provided to the draft model. However, in practice these layers are usually selected by simple fixed rules (e.g., positional heuristics) rather than an explicit objective that balances informativeness and redundancy. This creates both practical and scientific gap. Practically, multi-layer selection is combinatorial. For 36layer model, choosing only three layers yields thousands of combinations, and the search space grows rapidly for larger tuples. Scientifically, it remains unclear which layer combinations are jointly informative versus geometrically redundant. As result, default position-based heuristics (uniform selection with the initial and final layers offset) may perform well in some regimes without providing principled explanation of when or why they work. In this work, we view multi-layer hidden-state selection through the lenses of information maximization and * Equal Contribution Qualcomm AI Research is an initiative of Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. 1 tor that utilizes beam search to create informative layer sets. We introduce ELSI-C, an entropy-initialized CKAtransition extension for diversity-aware expansion. We introduce calibration token-entropy filtering, where hidden states of low predictive-entropy tokens are removed to sharpen layer-discriminative statistics. We demonstrate practical gains for EAGLE3-style conditioning using ELSI/ELSI-C-selected sets relative to the default [N 1] and [2, //2, 3] rules, while improving interpretability.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Layer specialization and redundancy in transformers. Prior work shows that transformer layers are not uniformly useful and that representational redundancy is often concentrated in middle layers. Transformer layerfunction studies report that many middle layers are partially interchangeable, while early and late layers remain more functionally distinct [1]. Related pruning/acceleration work similarly finds that substantial middlelayer computation can be removed with limited quality loss [2]. Representation-geometry analyses also suggest structured evolution of hidden states across depth [3, 4]. These studies motivate transition-aware reasoning: the depth axis can be divided into coherent compartments separated by sharp representational changes. To algorithmically identify these compartments, we introduce CKAtransition diagnostics. Spectral and rank-based analyses. complementary line of research studies rank and spectral structure for finetuning and compression. Adaptive rank-allocation methods for LoRA finetuning [5] demonstrate that rank requirements vary by layer/module and should not be treated uniformly [6, 7]. Other methods use low-rank approximations of transformer components for eﬀiciency [8]. Random-matrix and singular-value analyses further show that spectral tails and non-dominant directions can materially affect behavior [9]. However, these works primarily deal with over-parameterization and compression - they do not address the problem of selection of sets of activations. Figure 1: Prompt-wise per-layer Shannon entropy curves for Qwen3-4B-Instruct. The curves show depthwise non-uniform profile (an activation wave), with distinct early (06), middle (728), and late-layer (29 35) regimes. redundancy minimization. We use matrix entropy to quantify informativeness of layer sets and linear CKA to quantify representational redundancy. We first introduce Entropy-based Layer Set Iteration (ELSI), practical entropy-based procedure that scales to realistic model depths. ELSI uses beam search to eﬀiciently identify high-entropy layer sets by evaluating entropy on concatenated hidden states across layers. We then introduce ELSI-C, an entropy-initialized CKA-transition extension that promotes diversity-aware layer expansion. Alongside ELSI/ELSI-C, we introduce token-entropy filtering during calibration: hidden states of low predictiveentropy tokens are removed so that selection statistics focus on significant and informative positions. We empirically study Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Our analyses reveal consistent trends across both models: (i) non-uniform per-layer Shannon entropy profile (an activation wave across depth, Fig. 1), (ii) non-uniform entropy gain under layer concatenation, and (iii) CKA transition boundaries that indicate depth-wise representational compartments. These observations motivate ELSI, an entropy-based selector, and ELSI-C, diversity-aware extension. Moreover, they clarify why fixed baselines can still be competitive when they overlap with high-scoring entropy-beam regions. Contributions. We propose principled framework for studying and selecting multiple target-model hidden layers using matrix entropy of concatenated representations and CKA transitions between depths. We introduce ELSI, practical entropy-based selecSpeculative decoding and hidden-state conditioning. Recent speculative decoding frameworks such as EAGLE [10, 11] and DFlash [12] condition draft models on selected target-model hidden states. In current practice, those target layers are usually chosen by fixed, positionbased heuristics (e.g., [N 1] or [2, //2, 3]) which 2 may lead to redundant representations. Our work addresses this gap through ELSI, which maximizes information and diversity through matrix entropy and CKAtransition structure signals for principled multi-layer selection. We further introduce beam-overlap diagnostics to explain when and why position-based baseline rules still remain competitive. Positioning of this work. Relative to prior layeranalysis and rank-based compression literature, our contribution is to jointly optimize hidden-layer sets for downstream draft conditioning: (i) quantify set informativeness via entropy of fused representations with ELSI, (ii) control redundancy via CKA-transition-guided expansion with ELSI-C, and (iii) evaluate practical gains in EAGLE3-style speculative decoding with interpretable diagnostics.

sections.title: Method
sections.content: Qwen3-4B-Instruct Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct We first analyze per-layer Shannon matrix entropy S1. In Figure 2, we see that across models, entropy varies substantially with depth, indicating non-uniform layer informativeness. Llama3.1-8B-IT shows high entropy for the first layer which then drops sharply and then rises, peaking around layer 27. Based on this we add another condition when selecting single layer: in addition to having high-entropy, the layer index should occur after the middle layer index. Qwen3-4B-IT shows high-lowhigh entropy peaking at layer 28. While per-layer entropy can inform the selection of single layer, it does not immediately reveal favorable sets of layers, motivating deeper analysis. sections.title: 5.2 Entropy of layer pairs
sections.content: We next evaluate the entropy of concatenations of layer pairs. Figure 3 visualizes top-k seed layers (by per-layer entropy) against all companion layer concatenations. We see non-uniform gain patterns: some layer pairs provide strong complementary directions while others are largely redundant. Moreover, different seed layers benefit from different companion layers. These results justify the need to optimize sets of layers jointly and entropy of concatenated representations as metric to achieve this.

sections.title: 5.6.1 Baselines and Evaluation.
sections.content: We train EAGLE-style draft models using ELSI and ELSI-C and compare against layer selections based on: (i) EAGLE2 [N 1], (ii) EAGLE3 [2, //2, 3], and (iii) low-entropy negative sets.

sections.title: 5.6.2 Training and Evaluation Setup.
sections.content: All the draft models were trained using distillation dataset generated using ShareGPT [15] and Ultrachat [18] on 8 H100 GPUs. For evaluation we ablate over (a) number of draft tree nodes: 30 and 60, and (b) temperature sampling: T=0.0 (greedy) and T=1.0. We evaluate on SpecBench [19], which covers wide range of tasks and report average accepted tokens (τ ). Note that average accepted tokens will directly lead to higher token per second in this scenario for same number of hidden-states chosen. For smaller set of target states, we expect higher (a) Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (b) Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Figure 5: Pairwise CKA with calculated transition boundary overlaid in yellow. 6 throughput due to the usage of smaller down-projection layer of size Ld d, though this might not be visible on GPUs which are not memory-bound. We leave it to future work to experiment with ELSI-generated layer sets on edge-devices. We show our main results for Qwen3-4B-IT in Table 2 and make several observations in this data: ELSI (m=3), matching the number of EAGLE3 layers, is the best performing method on average across all settings, improving over EAGLE3 by 1.62.2% (+0.085 τ on average) and over EAGLE2 by 6.17.3%. Across all four settings, ELSI (m=1) matches or exceeds EAGLE3 on average (+0.01 to +0.04 τ ), showing that single well-chosen layer matches EAGLE3s default 3-layer heuristic. ELSI tends to provide the most benefit in categories where EAGLE3 performs weakest, for example Translation (2.65.6%) and Summarization (2.14.2%), but can also improve acceptance rate significantly in performant categories such as STEM (2.43.9%). ELSI provides consistent benefits across sampling temperatures and draft tree sizes configurations, and thus may be applied to diverse deployment scenarios. We also include low-entropy control experiment wherein we choose the layer set with the lowest entropy resulting in layers {0, 1, 35}). We train an EAGLE-3 model with this configuration and see that it consistently results in the lowest acceptance rate. This shows that using low entropy hidden-states (which could have overlapping information) doesnt provide strong conditioning to the draft model. 3 rate

Entropy-guided selection remains highly eﬀicient on this model: ELSI (m=1) exceeds EAGLE2 by 2.84.9% while attaining 99.0% of EAGLE3s block eﬀiciency using single hidden state rather than three. However, increasing the number of selected layers yields no further gain, with AVG varying by only 0.017 τ across = 1, 2, 3. On average, ELSI (m=3) trails EAGLE3 by 1.0%. However, at =1.0, ELSI (m=3) improves over EAGLE3 on Roleplay by 4.75.9% and on Coding by 3.03.3%, whereas at =0.0 the two are closer. The corresponding losses on Writing at =1.0 leave the average unchanged. We attribute the reduced headroom overall to the greater interchangeability of Llamas decoder layers, visible as broad regions of high pairwise CKA in Figure 5. When neighboring layers encode similar information, the choice of layers matters correspondingly less, and uniformly spaced selection already performs well. Framing layer selection through ELSI thus allows us to identify these differing regimes across models: where representations are diverse, selection results in significant benefits, and where they are redundant, it instead allows for smaller layer-set selection.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding through the lens of information maximization and geometric diversity, moving beyond Our analysis of defixed, positional heuristics. coder representations across Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct revealed consistent structural signals: non-uniform entropy profile across layers (the activation wave), non-uniform entropy gains with layer concatenation, and CKA transition boundaries that indicate distinct representational compartments. Tothese observations motivate joint selection of gether, layer sets to maximize information and minimize redundancy, instead of relying on hand-crafted layer indices. Building on these signals, we introduced ELSI and ELSIC as practical algorithms to select layer combinations for typical model sizes. We further enhanced these algorithms by introducing token-entropy filtering to reduce cross-prompt entropy variance, improving the stability of selection statistics. Empirically, we demonstrate (i) choice of layers matters more than the number of layers, and (ii) layer selection can result in sets that outperform EAGLE2 and EAGLE3 baselines. We further provide analysis of why currently used layer combinations do perform well in practice, thus enhancing the interpretability of current speculative decoding techniques. Overall, this work provides practical and interpretable framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection in speculative decoding. This framework is designed to be general, with the potential for future work that experiments with broader variety of target models and draft-model conditioning strategies. Further, the selection of sets of layers may find application in broader range of tasks beyond speculative decoding including embedding tasks and interpretability, and we encourage these as future directions for exploration.
